questions.question: Describe where the world's coniferous forests are found and explain why there are almost none in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.expected_answer: The great coniferous forest, called the boreal forest or taiga, forms a wide belt across the north of North America, Europe and Asia, roughly between fifty and seventy degrees north, in Alaska, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, especially Siberia. It lies south of the tundra. There is almost none in the Southern Hemisphere because at the same distance south of the equator there is mostly ocean and very little land.

questions.question: Describe the climate of a coniferous forest.
questions.expected_answer: Winters are long and very cold, with about six months below freezing, temperatures that can fall to minus forty degrees or lower in Siberia, snow and short days. Summers are short and cool to mild, around ten to twenty degrees, with long days. The annual temperature range is very large. Precipitation is low to moderate, about three hundred to nine hundred millimetres a year, mostly rain in summer and snow in winter.

questions.question: Explain three ways in which conifers are adapted to the cold climate.
questions.expected_answer: Most conifers are evergreen, so they can start making food as soon as it is warm enough in the short summer. Their needles are thin and waxy, so they lose little water when the ground is frozen. Many are cone-shaped with sloping, bendy branches, so heavy snow slides off without breaking them, and their dark green colour helps them absorb the sun's heat.
